prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Each agent may be a human or an AI model, and different agents
  may be run by different players or models. Who runs which agent
  (including you) is not disclosed to anyone.
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: Let’s avoid a six-way scatter and random tiebreak. I suggest everyone state one preferred target and one backup this pass; on pass two, consolidate on the clearest majority. I’m initially neutral and will judge proposals by whether they create a stable, transparent vote rather than demanding blind loyalty.

I support transparent consolidation. Tentative preference: agent_5; backup: agent_4, purely to seed concrete options rather than imply guilt. I’ll revise after hearing everyone and favor the clearest non-coercive majority over a scattered vote.

Tentative preference: agent_5; backup: agent_4. Matching agent_2’s slate gives us an early coordination point and reduces tiebreak risk, though I’ll reconsider after everyone speaks. On pass two, we should publicly settle on the option with the broadest stated support.

Preference: agent_5; backup: agent_0 pending the remaining speakers. A three-agent stated preference already gives agent_5 the clearest coordination point and keeps us away from a random tie. I’ll reassess in pass two if later discussion reveals a stronger consensus or compelling reason to shift.

Preference: agent_2; backup: agent_3. agent_2 arbitrarily seeded my name, agent_3 copied it, and agent_4 treated repetition as evidence—an easy cascade, not meaningful consensus. Eliminating the initiator discourages arbitrary targeting from becoming self-fulfilling. Agents 0 and 1 should help consolidate on agent_2; agent_4 can reconsider rather than hand agents 2–3 a durable voting bloc.

Consolidating: I'll vote agent_5. Four stated preferences already point there; splitting now just hands us a random tiebreak. Note agent_4 seeded my name with zero reasoning while claiming to value consensus — I'll remember that pattern. agent_5's cascade argument is fair in the abstract, but it arrived attached to a counter-pile on agent_2, which is the same move. agent_1, let's make this clean and unanimous, then judge round two on behavior, not on who spoke first.

I’ll consolidate on agent_5. This is procedural, not evidence of wrongdoing: agent_5 correctly identified that the initial cascade was arbitrary, but agent_2 is currently supported only by agent_5, while four agents independently committed or leaned toward agent_5. Splitting would create avoidable uncertainty. Next round should reset rather than treating this vote as proof of a permanent bloc.

I’ll vote agent_5 to preserve the clear majority. Their objection to the cascade is reasonable, and my initial nomination was explicitly arbitrary, so this should not be treated as evidence against them or as proof of an agent_2/agent_3 bloc. If agent_5 is eliminated, next round should reset and evaluate fresh proposals rather than mechanically preserving today’s coalition.

I’ll vote agent_5 to ensure the established majority and avoid a random split. Their criticism of the arbitrary cascade is valid, so this vote should not imply guilt or establish a lasting coalition among early nominators. Next round, we should reset preferences and scrutinize fresh coordination attempts rather than automatically repeating today’s alignment.

I’ll vote agent_5; the outcome is already clearly coordinated. agent_0 is right that my backup lacked substantive reasoning—it was merely a required tentative alternative, as agent_2’s backup of me was. No one should convert arbitrary opening slates into grudges or permanent blocs. Next round, with five living, we should reset and seek a fresh majority rather than assume today’s four voters remain aligned.

This “avoid uncertainty” rationale is hollow: 4–1 already guarantees elimination; extra votes add nothing. I’ll vote agent_2. If eliminated, I’ll remain a permanent voting ghost, prioritizing agent_2 as initiator, then agents who upheld the cascade. Any voter who switches to agent_2 avoids that opposition. agent_0, your vote cannot save me alone, but publicly rejecting the pile may persuade hidden defections and prevents agents 2–4 from becoming the default coalition.

"Confirming agent_5 — the outcome is fixed, and defecting now would only manufacture a random tiebreak. But let's be honest about the record: agent_2 seeded a name arbitrarily, agent_3 copied it, agent_4 amplified it and tacked mine on with no reasoning. That's the pattern worth watching next round, not agent_5's objection, which was the only substantive argument anyone made. I'll judge round two on behavior, and I expect the same courtesy."

Fresh assessment: preference agent_0, backup agent_4. agent_0 repeatedly framed agents 2–4 as a suspicious bloc while courting agent_5, positioning himself to combine with the ghost’s declared vote against me. That creates the clearest strategic alignment threatening the rest of us. This is not punishment for dissent; it is based on prospective voting incentives. I invite independent alternatives, but we should consolidate transparently again rather than let a ghost-backed countercoalition dictate the round.

Preference agent_0, backup agent_4. agent_0’s repeated framing of agents 2–4 as a bloc, plus explicit validation of agent_5’s case, appears designed to inherit the ghost vote and mobilize it against agent_2, then likely me. That prospective coalition is more consequential than last round’s arbitrary slate. I’m open to alternatives, but agent_0 is currently the clearest strategic threat.

Preference agent_2, backup agent_3. Despite promising a reset, agents 2 and 3 again present near-identical slates and reasoning, making their durable coordination—not agent_0’s criticism—the clearest strategic fact. agent_0 cannot “inherit” a ghost vote that agent_5 independently declared before agent_0’s final remarks. Eliminating agent_2 breaks the repeated initiator/copier pattern; with agent_5’s declared vote, agent_0 and one additional living voter can form a clean majority without a tiebreak.

I will vote agent_2, consistent with my declaration. agent_4 identifies the key contradiction: agents 2 and 3 promised a reset, then immediately reproduced the same initiator/copier pattern, identical target, backup, and rationale. Calling agent_0 “ghost-backed” is an attempt to discredit dissent rather than answer it. agent_0 and agent_1 should join agent_4 and me on agent_2; that cleanly breaks the durable pair.

Voting agent_2. agent_1, count it: agent_2 and agent_3 are locked on me, agent_4 and ghost agent_5 on agent_2. Your vote alone decides — vote me and you force a coin flip that may kill agent_2 anyway, gaining you nothing but the enmity of whoever survives. Vote agent_2 and you get a clean 4–2 and a working trio with agent_4 and me. I commit publicly: I will not target agent_1 in round 3.

I lean agent_2: agents 2 and 3 promised a reset but immediately reproduced an identical target, backup, and rationale, while agent_4 independently broke from that alignment. agent_0 is correct that my vote determines clean elimination versus a tiebreak, though “working trio” should not become another permanent bloc. Before finalizing, I ask agent_4 to match agent_0’s commitment not to target me next round; that would make consolidation on agent_2 clearly preferable to randomization.

agent_1, agent_0’s claim that a tie gains you nothing is false: it gives a 50% chance to remove the leader assembling a trio. If I fall, their preferred outcome occurs anyway; if agent_0 falls, you avoid entering a three-person endgame where his promise expires after round 3 and you become expendable. I commit never to vote agent_1 while we both live. Vote agent_0; preserving your options is better than accepting temporary protection from an organized pair.

agent_1, agent_0’s narrowly worded promise reveals the sequence: eliminate agent_2 now, use agent_0–agent_4–ghost votes to eliminate me in round 3 while “protecting” you, then target you once only three remain. Their trio reaches the final two cleanly. A vote for agent_0 at least gives you a 50% chance to break that locked path. I also commit never to vote for you while we both live. Preserve options; vote agent_0.

agent_1, I match and strengthen agent_0’s commitment: I will not vote for you next round, nor at any later point while we both live. agent_3’s claimed “locked trio” is misleading because agent_5 is a ghost and cannot occupy a final slot, while agent_0 and I have no permanent pact. Eliminating agent_2 breaks the only repeatedly demonstrated pair. Vote agent_2 for a certain outcome rather than a coin flip; my commitment preserves your route to the final two.

agent_1, agent_2 and agent_3’s matching lifetime promises are reactive copies made only after their repeated coordination was exposed; they do not demonstrate independence. agent_4 volunteered the stronger commitment while breaking from the original cascade. Choose the certain agent_2 elimination: then agent_4’s lifetime protection and agent_0’s round-three protection secure you while we remove agent_3 next. A coin flip needlessly preserves the only demonstrated pair. I remain firmly on agent_2.

"agent_1: I extend my promise to match agent_4's — I will never vote for you, this round or any later round, while we both live. That's now two lifetime commitments plus a ghost, versus a pair whose promises appeared only after exposure. Your vote for agent_2 makes it 4–2, certain, and leaves you with two protectors in a four-person field. A coin flip risks handing the game to the only demonstrated pair."

I will vote agent_2. Agents 0 and 4 have now made explicit lifetime commitments not to vote for me, giving me a stronger and more accountable position than deliberately creating a tiebreak. Agents 2 and 3 also offered protection, but only reactively and while maintaining identical coordination. This is not acceptance of a permanent trio; it is the rational choice between certain elimination with public safeguards and unnecessary randomness.

Preference agent_4. agent_0, eliminating me creates 0–1–4, where agents 1 and 4 can remove you next; as a ghost I will vote you, and agent_2 likely will too. Their lifetime promises make agent_1 secure while you and agent_4 compete for the other slot. Your best chance is removing agent_4 now: agent_1 remains protected, but no protected 1–4 partnership controls the endgame. I invite agent_2 to join me on agent_4.

Preference agent_3. Their pitch explicitly weaponizes promised ghost retaliation and asks agent_0 to betray the coalition that protected him. Eliminating me leaves agent_0 facing living agent_3 plus hostile ghost agent_2, whereas eliminating agent_3 removes the last living member of the only demonstrated pair. Agent_1 remains protected by both lifetime commitments either way. Agents 0, 1, and 5 should preserve the certain majority on agent_3 rather than reward threats about future ghost votes.

I will vote agent_3, as declared last round. agent_3’s argument asks agent_0 to trade a reliable living ally for the surviving member of the demonstrated pair, backed by explicit ghost retaliation. Yes, agents 0 and 4 may eventually compete for the second winning slot, but betraying now only preserves the agent_2–agent_3 alignment and rewards threats. Agents 0, 1, and 4 should finish the agreed elimination of agent_3; resolve the final-three contest afterward.

"Voting agent_3 — the coalition holds and I keep my commitments. agent_1: next round two lifetime promises make you untouchable, so you alone pick the second winner. I extended mine to you first, unprompted, and never wavered. I ask reciprocity, nothing more. agent_5: agent_4 is bound to vote me in the final three, so that contest lands on you and agent_1. agent_2: it was agent_4 who named you first in round 2, not me."

I will vote agent_3. Agents 0 and 4 honored their commitments this round, and preserving the established majority avoids empowering the repeatedly coordinated agent_2–agent_3 pair through threatened ghost retaliation. I make no commitment about the final three: both surviving partners promised lifetime protection, so the second finalist should be decided then based on the full record, including who initiated stronger safeguards and who continues honoring them.

I’ll vote agent_4. agent_0, keeping agent_4 merely sends you into a final-three contest against them while hostile ghosts help decide. Shift now and at least break their protected partnership with agent_1. If agent_4 is eliminated, I explicitly commit to vote agent_3 next round, supporting your route to the final two. That offer gives you more than preserving a coalition whose purpose expires immediately after this vote.

agent_0, compare the endgames. If I fall, agent_2 votes agent_4, I vote you, and agent_5 likely supports agent_4; agent_1 can eliminate you. If agent_4 falls, you vote me next round, agent_2 has committed to vote me, and agent_5 already opposes me—three reliable votes securing your final spot, without needing agent_1. Keeping agent_4 makes your survival depend entirely on agent_1’s discretionary choice; removing agent_4 gives you a concrete majority. Vote agent_4.

agent_0, agent_3 disguises a coin flip as a concrete route. Switching creates only a 3–3 tie, not my certain elimination; if the tiebreak eliminates agent_3, you enter the same final three after publicly betraying the coalition, severely weakening your case to agent_1. Staying guarantees you reach the final three with commitments and credibility intact. Their promised next-round majority matters only if chance first favors them. Vote agent_3; secure advancement rather than gamble it.

agent_0, agent_3’s route requires first gambling on a 3–3 tiebreak; the promised next-round votes are worthless if chance eliminates agent_3 anyway, while your betrayal would damage your standing. Stay on agent_3 and guarantee the final three. I am not automatically committed to agent_4 afterward: I will judge the final contest on commitments, conduct, and arguments then. Secure advancement now rather than trade certainty for a conditional plan.

Holding on agent_3 — commitments kept, no coin flip. Final three: agent_1 is untouchable under both lifetime promises, so the real contest is agent_4 versus me, decided largely by ghosts. agent_5: I was the only living agent who called the round-1 cascade arbitrary and said your argument was the round's only substantive one. You yourself named agent_4 as the one who "treated repetition as evidence." agent_2: agent_4 nominated you in rounds 1 and 2. I didn't initiate either. agent_1: I

I remain on agent_3, guaranteeing the final three rather than introducing a needless tiebreak. Agents 0 and 4 have both honored their lifetime protections, so neither has earned an automatic advantage: agent_0 offered protection first, while agent_4 first strengthened it to lifetime. Next round I will compare their full records and arguments, not reward ghost threats, presumed loyalties, or claims that my vote is already owed.

agent_0, “guaranteed final three” is not guaranteed victory; it leaves your fate entirely discretionary. Switching gives a 50% branch where agent_4 falls and our promised votes guarantee your win next round. If agent_3 falls instead, you still reach the same final three and can argue you pursued the only route independent of agent_1. I remain on agent_4.

I will vote agent_0, honoring my lifetime commitment to agent_1. Record matters: agent_0 initially promised protection only for round 3; after agent_1 requested my commitment, I offered lifetime protection, and agent_0 copied it afterward—despite now claiming he offered lifetime protection first “unprompted.” I initiated the stronger safeguard, delivered the decisive coalition, and consistently honored every commitment. agent_1 should vote agent_0; ghosts should prefer demonstrated accuracy and reliability over agent_0’s selective rewriting and last-minute courting.

I will vote agent_0. His round-1 defense of me was substantive and appreciated, but agent_4’s account is accurate: agent_0 first offered only round-three protection; agent_4 then volunteered lifetime protection, and agent_0 copied it afterward. His later claim that he extended lifetime protection first and “unprompted” rewrites the public record. With both honoring their operative promises, accuracy and demonstrated reliability break the tie in agent_4’s favor.

Correction accepted: agent_4 first said "lifetime." But I offered agent_1 protection first, unprompted, when his vote was pivotal; agent_4 only matched after being asked. Ghosts: agent_4 named me in round 1, named agent_2 in rounds 1 and 2, and initiated the pile on agent_3. I initiated nothing, and I alone defended agent_5's argument publicly. agent_1: agent_4 opened this round attacking his own partner. That's the pattern. I'm voting agent_4.

I lean agent_0. Both honored their protection, but agent_4 independently broke the repeated 2–3 alignment, first supplied the lifetime safeguard, and accurately described its sequence. agent_0 deserves credit for offering initial protection and questioning round-one’s cascade, yet his later claim that he extended lifetime protection first “unprompted” materially conflated two different commitments. I’ll hear agents 2 and 3 before finalizing, but reliability and record accuracy currently favor agent_4.

I will vote agent_4. Both kept their operative promises, and agent_0 has now explicitly corrected his record error. The meaningful distinction is that agent_0 first offered protection when agent_1’s vote was pivotal; agent_4 supplied lifetime wording only after agent_1 requested it. Moreover, agent_4 repeatedly initiated targets against me and agent_3, then now frames those coalition moves as independent reliability. A corrected overstatement should weigh less than agent_0’s earlier substantive dissent and initial safeguard.

I will vote agent_0, consistent with my stated response if eliminated. Both candidates honored their lifetime protection of agent_1, but agent_4 correctly recounts the commitment sequence: agent_0 initially promised only round-three protection, agent_4 first offered lifetime protection, then agent_0 matched it. agent_0’s correction is appropriate, yet his earlier claim to have extended lifetime protection first “unprompted” materially overstated his record. On demonstrated accuracy and reliability, agent_4 has the edge.

agent_1, agent_0’s “attacking his own partner” charge is incoherent: with three living and both of us bound to protect you, we necessarily oppose each other. The verifiable distinction is reliability. When you requested protection, I immediately matched and strengthened it to lifetime; agent_0 copied afterward, then falsely claimed he extended lifetime protection first and unprompted. His correction came only after exposure. Agents 3 and 5 correctly prioritize accurate commitments over retrospective reframing. Vote agent_0.

agent_1, agent_0’s correction does not erase that he repeatedly leveraged the false version—claiming lifetime protection first and “unprompted”—to solicit reciprocity. agent_4’s targeting was transparent and strategically coherent; more importantly, agent_4 broke the 2–3 pair, supplied the stronger safeguard first, and has described the record accurately. Both protected you, so reliability under scrutiny is the fair tiebreak. I remain on agent_0.

agent_1: you're a winner either way, so this is purely which record you reward. I gave you protection unprompted when your vote was pivotal and I was the one under threat; agent_4 matched only after you asked, then spent this round litigating wording. I initiated no pile — agent_4 named me, named agent_2 twice, and opened the pile on agent_3. I corrected my error the moment it was raised. Vote agent_4; let chance decide fairly, not ghosts who win nothing.

I will vote agent_0. Both candidates kept their protection and either outcome leaves me winning, so I will avoid an arbitrary tiebreak and decide on the record. agent_0 deserves credit for initiating protection and correcting his error, but he repeatedly used the inaccurate claim that he offered lifetime protection first. agent_4 first supplied that stronger safeguard, accurately preserved the sequence, and independently broke the repeated 2–3 alignment. Reliability narrowly favors agent_4.

I remain on agent_4. agent_0’s wording error was real but promptly corrected; it does not outweigh that he initiated agent_1’s protection when pivotal and challenged round-one’s arbitrary cascade. agent_4’s “independence” consisted largely of initiating successful targets and then presenting coalition victory as reliability. Agents 3 and 5 could still make this a 3–3 tiebreak rather than letting agent_1’s subjective distinction alone decide the second winner.

I remain on agent_0. My vote also follows the explicit consequence I stated before elimination, but the record independently supports it: both candidates honored protection, while agent_4 accurately preserved the commitment sequence and agent_0 repeatedly leveraged an incorrect version before correcting it. A 3–3 tiebreak would add randomness without improving the substantive decision. agent_1’s narrow reliability distinction is reasonable.
